_note: Sofia's research file: what each site is, where the analogy breaks down, and how it helps exploration. Known sites: 'helps' = what has been tested there, with source links in 'sources'. New candidates: 'helps' = what we could test there (write it once the pipeline ranks them; only the ~5 shown in the demo). [brackets] = still to research or check. Coordinates in scores.csv are approximate. Gorafe and Kali Gandaki are parked per the criteria doc. 'zoom' = how close the 3D terrain view flies in (11 shows about 20 km, 14 about 2 km). 'outlook' = short Opportunities and Challenges lines; each line's 'src' lists 1-based numbers into that site's 'sources', or "ours" for our own pipeline measurement (outputs/raw_values.csv, config-v1).

Haughton Crater.why: About 20 km impact crater in a cold polar desert; long-running NASA analog site.
Haughton Crater.breaks: 24-hour sun during the summer field season, so no lasting shadow while crews are there.
Haughton Crater.helps: Haughton-Mars Project (since 1997, NASA-supported, run by the Mars Institute): field tests of rovers, including a pressurized rover with suit ports, robotic drills, cameras and spectrometers, spacesuit gear such as a smart glove, and long traverses planned like Moon and Mars expeditions.

sources.label: NASA Earth Observatory: Mars researchers rendezvous on remote Arctic island (Haughton-Mars Project)
Mars Institute: HMP
Aerospace Testing International: Testing for Mars in the High Arctic

validation.text: Haughton was a validation test: we ran our frozen method (config-v1) on it without tuning anything. It found no crater there. In the whole searched area (65 × 67 km) the elevation data shows no closed bowl, not even one 10 m deep. Haughton is about 20 km wide but heavily eroded, so it is no longer a bowl our method can see. Relief near the site is only 34–368 m.

Atacama (Yungay area).why: One of the driest places on Earth, with very high UV.
Atacama (Yungay area).breaks: Warm and near the tropics: no polar lighting and no long shadows.
Atacama (Yungay area).helps: NASA's ARADS project (from 2016) drove the KREX-2 prototype rover near Yungay, drilled up to 2 m and tested life-detection instruments (SOLID, Wet Chemistry Lab) to rehearse a search for life on Mars.

Meteor Crater.why: About 1.2 km wide impact crater; Apollo astronauts trained in geology here.
Meteor Crater.breaks: Hot desert at mid-latitude: no polar light, far smaller than Shackleton.
Meteor Crater.helps: Apollo astronauts did geology field training here from 1963, taught by USGS scientists such as Gene Shoemaker. The crater is still used to train astronauts for missions to the lunar south pole.

opportunities.text: NASA's Artemis geology training has a field camp at Meteor Crater or another lunar-analog site, with a simulated moonwalk on real geology.
In 2025 science teams tested a backpack lidar (3D mapping) and a ground-penetrating radar here ahead of a Moon landing.
Our data: the most Moon-like bowl we found, with walls of about 24° and 99% drivable ground within 5 km.

challenges.text: Privately owned: the Barringer family's company still owns and runs the crater.
Visitors stay on paved rim paths; the public may not climb to the bottom because the slopes erode and are unstable.
About 1 km wide, while some craters on the Moon are hundreds of kilometres wide.

Craters of the Moon.why: Young basalt lava field with lava tubes; Apollo astronauts trained here in 1969.
Craters of the Moon.breaks: Young, fresh lava with plants, air and weather. Lunar basalt is buried under fine dust (regolith) built up over billions of years of impacts.
Craters of the Moon.helps: On 22 August 1969, Apollo 14 crew Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell, with Joe Engle and Eugene Cernan, learned volcanic geology here to pick the most valuable rock samples on the Moon. NASA scientists still do research here.

sources.label: National Park Service: Space exploration research and astronaut training

Lava Beds.place: Lava Beds National Monument, California, USA
Lava Beds.why: Hundreds of lava-tube caves in basalt.
Lava Beds.breaks: Earth caves have air, moisture, ice and microbes, and they are much smaller than the lava tubes thought to exist on the Moon.
Lava Beds.helps: NASA Ames's BRAILLE project (2019) drove the CaveR rover in Valentine Cave to map the cave with a laser scanner and look for signs of microbial life on the walls, showing that a remotely operated rover can explore a lava tube.

sources.label: NASA Astrobiology: Using a cave rover, NASA learns to search for life underground (2019)

Lanzarote lava tubes.why: Lava tubes and volcanic plains; ESA trains astronauts in planetary geology on the island.
Lanzarote lava tubes.breaks: Mild ocean climate with air and weather, and a tourist island with roads and towns, so it is far easier to reach than a lunar cave.
Lanzarote lava tubes.helps: ESA's PANGAEA course trains astronauts from ESA, NASA and JAXA in planetary geology here, including work inside the Corona lava tube, one of the largest volcanic caves on Earth.

sources.label: ESA: Turning astronauts into planetary explorers (2023)

pinacate r001c002.name: El Elegante crater
pinacate r001c002.place: El Pinacate y Gran Desierto de Altar, Sonora, Mexico
pinacate r001c002.why: A near-circular volcanic crater (maar) about 1.6 km wide and 244 m deep, with steep inner walls and a flat floor: our pipeline's closest bowl after Meteor Crater.
pinacate r001c002.breaks: It is a volcanic maar, made by steam explosions, not an impact crater. Hot, low-latitude desert: no polar light or permanent shadow, and far smaller than Shackleton (about 21 km).

opportunities.text: Apollo astronauts trained for lunar exploration in the Pinacate volcanic field, with University of Arizona geologists.
The reserve has ten large, almost perfectly circular maar craters, so several bowls can be compared in one field campaign.
Our data: our closest bowl after Meteor Crater, about 1.5 km wide and 215 m deep, with 98% of the rim drivable.

challenges.text: Protected: a UNESCO World Heritage site (2013) under the authority of Mexico's federal protected-areas agency, CONANP.
In 2022, blockades by communal landowners cut off parts of the reserve, including its visitor centre.

arid_al_wahbah r001c001.name: Al Wahbah crater
arid_al_wahbah r001c001.place: Harrat Kishb, Makkah Province, Saudi Arabia
arid_al_wahbah r001c001.why: A deep, round volcanic crater (maar) about 2 km wide and 220–250 m deep, with a white salt floor; about 1.1 million years old. Our pipeline measured it at 2.2 km wide and 165 m deep from rim to floor.
arid_al_wahbah r001c001.breaks: Volcanic maar from a steam explosion, not an impact crater. At 23° N the Sun climbs to the zenith, so there is no low polar light and no lasting shadow on the floor.
arid_al_wahbah r001c001.helps: [to write once ranked: what we could test here]

opportunities.text: Visitors already hike down to the white salt floor, so the whole bowl can be reached on foot.
Our data: the widest bowl in our results (about 2.2 km, 165 m deep), with almost bare ground (99.8%) and 97% drivable within 5 km.

challenges.text: The official tourism site says it is reachable only through tour operators.
Most visitors come in the cooler winter and spring months.

arid_roter_kamm r001c001.name: Roter Kamm crater
arid_roter_kamm r001c001.why: A real impact crater, about 2.5 km wide and 4–5 million years old, with a rim about 130 m above its floor. Our pipeline measured it at 2.0 km wide and 82 m deep from rim to floor.
arid_roter_kamm r001c001.breaks: Wind-blown sand fills the floor at least 100 m deep, so it is much shallower than when it formed. Low-latitude desert (28° S): high Sun, no polar light. [check: access, it lies in a restricted diamond-mining area]

opportunities.text: A true impact crater, about 2.5 km wide and about 5 million years old.
Its sand fill, up to about 300 m thick, has been mapped with electromagnetic soundings: a test case for instruments that look under the ground.
Our data: fully bare ground and almost all of it drivable within 5 km.

challenges.text: It lies in Tsau ǁKhaeb (Sperrgebiet) National Park; in 2021 public access was still limited to a single tour concession.
In 2022 rangers did not allow a research team to drive into the crater, so all measurements inside were done on foot.

Tenoumer crater.why: A confirmed impact crater about 1.9 km wide and about 110 m deep from rim crest to floor (300–400 m when it formed, before sand filled it). Our search covered it (region arid_tenoumer, cell r001c001) but found no crater there.
Tenoumer crater.breaks: Our pipeline measures a crater's spill depth: how deep it is up to the lowest point of its rim, where water would overflow. Tenoumer's rim is low or sanded over on one side, so its spill depth is only 44 m, just under our 50 m minimum (settings config-v1). We kept the limit: changing it to let a known crater through would be tuning the method to the answer.
Tenoumer crater.helps: It shows a real limitation of config-v1 and the fix for the next version: filter by rim-crest depth instead of the lowest saddle, so old, sand-filled craters like Tenoumer are not dropped.
